summary: Reinforcement learning has achieved remarkable success in sequential decision-making, but learning effective policies often requires substantial interaction experience. Model-based reinforcement learning alleviates this dependence by leveraging world models, which are typically used to support planning or policy optimization. In this paper, we investigate an alternative paradigm in which autonomous LLM-based coding agents directly synthesize control policies by reasoning over readable world models. By examining environment source code, these agents translate environmental knowledge into executable decision rules and iteratively refine their policies using online feedback or offline data, without task-specific RL training. Experiments across diverse decision-making benchmarks show that synthesized policies match or outperform conventional RL methods while requiring substantially less experience. Further analyses reveal interpretable decision rules and how they evolve through feedback-driven refinement. Comparisons with policies generated without source code access and experiments under challenging conditions further demonstrate the benefits of readable world models. These findings suggest that direct policy synthesis can reduce reliance on trial and error, challenging the necessity of task-specific RL training.

title: Nav4Manip: From Navigation to Dexterous Mobile Manipulation through Co-Evolution
summary: Dexterous mobile manipulation is essential for robots to perform useful tasks in complex, unstructured environments. However, existing systems face two challenges. First, navigation remains too coarse for downstream manipulation, which often requires a precise base position and approach orientation rather than merely reaching a meter-scale goal region. Second, navigation and manipulation are commonly trained in isolation, lacking a feedback loop that enables the two capabilities to co-evolve. These limitations prevent current systems from reliably executing long-horizon dexterous mobile-manipulation tasks in real-world environments. To address them, we introduce Nav4Manip, a bidirectionally coupled co-evolution system for long-horizon dexterous mobile manipulation. It comprises two complementary architectures: Nav4Manip-N learns long-horizon navigation and refines its policy through manipulation feedback, while Nav4Manip-M trains a world-action model (WAM) for downstream dexterous manipulation. We train Nav4Manip-N in three stages: multi-task co-tuning learns navigation behavior and manipulation-aware affordance prediction; rejection sampling fine-tuning (RFT) rejects low-quality policy-generated paths and fine-tunes the model on retained trajectories; and reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF) uses counterfactual preferences to further improve navigation decisions. To support this framework, we establish the Nav-N-Manip benchmark and construct Nav4Manip-Pairs from benchmark rollouts, providing large-scale paired navigation--manipulation trajectories and affordance supervision. Extensive experiments on public vision-language navigation (VLN) benchmarks and Nav-N-Manip demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, while real-world evaluations show that Nav4Manip completes diverse dexterous mobile-manipulation tasks. Project website: https://nav4manip.github.io/.

title: Distractor-Robust Reinforcement Learning via Variational Bisimulation
summary: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) promises data efficiency and generalization, but typical reconstruction-based objectives encourage models to waste representational capacity on task-irrelevant distractors. We introduce VIBES (Variational Inference for Bisimulation-based Encoded States), a new objective that replaces pixel reconstruction with an adversarial term, which enforces that latent states suffice to predict both rewards and the next latent state. We show that this objective measures how far the encoder is from reward and dynamics sufficiency, and that whenever exact sufficiency is attainable, its global optima induce bisimulation relations on histories. Combined with a fixed-capacity latent bottleneck, this encourages latent states to retain task-relevant information while discarding irrelevant variation. Our method serves as a drop-in replacement for Dreamer's model-learning component, achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Distracting Control Suite, and extends to visually complex manipulation in Realistic ManiSkill. Unlike prior approaches, it does not rely on image-specific augmentations and applies equally well to high-dimensional vector-state tasks, demonstrated on a 100-link swimmer robot. Finally, latent-space analyses (UMAP embeddings and nearest-neighbor probes) confirm that the learned representations are sensitive to task-relevant structure while invariant to distractors.

title: Data-enhanced self-learning projective quantum Monte Carlo with Rydberg-atom measurements
summary: We introduce a data-enhanced self-learning projective quantum Monte Carlo (PQMC) method that incorporates projective measurements from programmable quantum simulators into the guiding wavefunction of a ground-state projection. We demonstrate the approach for a two-dimensional Rydberg-atom array using restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM) and recurrent neural network (RNN) guiding wavefunctions. Experimental pretraining reduces finite-population effects and accelerates self-learning convergence, allowing unbiased estimation of ground-state properties to be obtained with fewer walkers and fewer self-learning iterations. The improvement is particularly pronounced for the RBM, while the more accurate RNN guiding wavefunction exhibits a smaller, though still observable, benefit from pretraining. Simulations across different system sizes suggest that the relative advantage of experimental pretraining may increase with system size. Improvements are also observed for the checkerboard order parameter, despite deviations of the experimental measurements from the equilibrium numerical results. Finally, finite-size scaling with self-learning PQMC without experimental pretraining yields the critical point and critical exponents of the disordered-to-checkerboard transition in agreement with previous numerical studies. Our results show that limited and imperfect experimental measurements can provide an effective initialization for self-learning PQMC, while imaginary-time projection combined with subsequent unsupervised learning progressively refines the guiding wavefunction toward the ground state.

title: ZeroHero: Training Small Language Agents from Scratch
summary: Large pretrained language models provide capable policies for interactive tasks, but how much model capacity is necessary for a specialized language agent? We introduce ZeroHero, a framework for training small language agents (SLAs) from scratch. In each environment, a large language model acts as the expert, and we collect its successful trajectories. We pretrain each SLA, which has fewer than 50 million parameters, to predict the expert's responses given the interaction history. We then post-train the agent on its own interactions using proximal policy optimization (PPO). During post-training, reasoning alignment supplements environment rewards with expert supervision on the language the agent generates alongside its actions. We evaluate the agents in three multistep environments where acting requires both understanding and generating language. In Crafter, agents interpret textual observations and generate reasoning before acting. In WebShop, they translate shopping instructions into search queries. In Alfworld-Dialogue, they ask clarifying questions and use the answers to guide household actions. The agents approach expert performance on WebShop and surpass their respective demonstration experts on Crafter training rollouts and held-out Alfworld-Dialogue tasks. An interactive demo is available at https://zoyav.github.io/-ZoyaV-zerohero-demo.

title: LatentRL-QAS: Transfer via Latent Reinforcement Learning for Quantum Architecture Search
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) emerges as a prominent approach to quantum architecture search (QAS), the automated design of quantum circuits. However, transferring what an agent has learned from one number of qubits to another is still weakly explored: the state, the action space and the neural network of a state-of-the-art RL-QAS agent all grow with the number of qubits, which makes transfer learning across qubit counts prohibitive. We make this transfer possible by introducing LatentRL-QAS, a latent space transfer and refresh framework for RL-based QAS. At its core, a circuit variational autoencoder encodes a circuit as one token per gate and maps circuits on any number of qubits into the same latent space. An RL agent navigates this space instead of adding gates, so its state, actions and network have the same size at every qubit count. The latent space is periodically refreshed with the agent's new discoveries and, for a larger system, grown from the solutions of the smaller one, so what is transferred is the representation of circuits, not network weights or past experience. To show transfer, we consider absolutely maximally entangled (AME) states, a resource for quantum error correction. LatentRL-QAS discovers the five- and six-qubit AME states without being shown them and prepares them in 89-99% of evaluation episodes, whereas the baseline RL-QAS fails to find them with the same budget, even with a network 10 to 17 times larger. LatentRL-QAS remains robust under depolarizing noise with single-qubit gate errors amplified 10x and two-qubit gate errors 5x compared with IBM quantum hardware. By decoupling the RL agent from the number of qubits, LatentRL-QAS lets quantum architecture search reuse circuit representations learned on smaller problems, providing a foundation for the transferable design of circuits across quantum optimization problems.

title: A Differential Computing Accelerator for LLM Inference Leveraging Bit-Slice Transition Sparsity
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) have become foundational to modern artificial intelligence. Driven by scaling laws, their rapid growth poses increasing computational and memory challenges for deployment. To accelerate the general matrix multiplication (GEMM) operations that dominate LLM computation, bit-slice architectures decompose quantized operands along the bit dimension, exposing slice-level sparsity and redundancy. However, existing bit-slice designs primarily exploit sparsity in high-order slices, while dense low-order slices still offer substantial untapped reuse opportunities.
  We observe that bit-slice vectors (BSVs) are highly clustered in Hamming space, with many BSVs lying only a few bit flips away from a small set of representative patterns. Based on this observation, we propose ISTS, an algorithm-hardware co-designed accelerator that leverages representative BSV patterns as shared Steiner points to reuse partial sums across slices, substantially reducing computation. Specifically, the partial sum of each target BSV can be reconstructed from that of its assigned Steiner point using only a few additions or subtractions. On the algorithmic side, we propose Steiner Absorption Table Construction (SATC), which selects a compact set of Steiner points to absorb BSVs with only a few bidirectional bit flips, while FlipPrune selectively prunes flips to further expand the reusable BSV population. On the hardware side, we design a lightweight accelerator that supports Steiner reuse for static linear layer weights and runtime-generated attention K/V tensors. Comprehensive evaluations show that ISTS achieves average speedups of $3.09\times$, $2.41\times$, $2.18\times$, $1.27\times$, and $1.41\times$ over the state-of-the-art accelerators ANT, BBS, LUT Tensor Core, Transitive Array, and MCBP-BRCR, respectively.

title: Investigation of generalization to unseen audio generation models in audio--text semantic-alignment score prediction
summary: Text-to-audio generation (TTA) requires reliable evaluation of semantic alignment between generated audio and input text. Existing learning-based alignment-score prediction models have been evaluated only on audio generated by models included in the training data, leaving their generalization to unseen generation models unexplored. In this paper, we investigate the generalization of audio--text semantic-alignment score prediction models to unseen TTA models and introduce adversarial training using a generation-model classifier with a gradient reversal layer (GRL). Experimental results show that pretrained audio encoders capture generation-model-specific characteristics and that alignment-score prediction performance degrades on audio generated by unseen TTA models. Applying the GRL improves prediction performance in some settings, although its effectiveness in suppressing generation-model-specific information is limited.

title: From Models to Services: Systematizing Security Assurance for Model-as-a-Service
summary: Large language models are mainly delivered as cloud services, in which the assets of different principals are coupled within a single service pipeline, while the related security research is scattered across several fields with differing threat models. This paper systematizes this research from a service perspective. We decompose Model-as-a-Service (MaaS) into a five-layer stack and five trust boundaries, define six adversary classes and six security goals, use them to code 120 studies, and evaluate 50 defenses under a unified set of criteria. The results show that 44.2% of the studies concentrate on behavioral integrity, while service integrity, availability and cost, and accountability together account for only 13.3%. Defenses are evaluated on production services at less than half the rate of attacks, and none of the cryptographic or hardware mechanisms that protect against the provider can be adopted unilaterally by customers. Finally, we propose a research agenda by comparison with current standards and regulations.

title: Evaluating More with Less: Black-Box Test Selection for AI Agents
summary: Agentic software systems are increasingly used in development, where changes to the model, prompt, scaffold, tools, or execution environment require repeated testing. Test case selection (TCS) can reduce testing costs while providing estimates of agent performance or exposing failures early. Although TCS has been studied for deep neural networks and LLM code models, prior work does not directly address agentic systems and often requires model information unavailable for proprietary agents. We present the first empirical study of black-box TCS for agentic software systems. We treat each benchmark task as a test case and adapt black-box regression-testing techniques using selection criteria based on task descriptions, metadata, code fragments, and embeddings. We also propose strategies that estimate task difficulty using heuristic features or independent LLM-as-judge assessments. Our strategies select tasks without executing the target agent or using past results. We evaluate fourteen selection strategies, including random sampling, plus a historical-data baseline, across ten AI agent benchmarks with 12 to 101 agents per benchmark. We assess Success Rate estimation and early failure detection. No single strategy dominates both objectives. Adapted black-box regression-testing strategies are most effective for Success Rate estimation, with Category Partition obtaining the lowest median error on five benchmarks at the 20% task budget. LLM-as-judge selection is more effective for early failure detection. For GPT 5.2 Codex on SWE-bench Verified, Category Partition selects 100 instead of 500 tasks, reducing execution cost from \$225 to \$47, with a Success Rate estimation error of 0.8 percentage points. At the same budget, LLM-as-judge selection detects nearly twice as many failures as random sampling: 53.0% of selected tasks reveal failures, compared with 27.4% for random sampling.

title: PipeAxes: Decoupling Compute and Communication Granularities for Pipeline-Parallel LLM Serving
summary:
Pipeline parallelism can serve long-context language models on PCIe servers and across heterogeneous GPU clusters. Existing engines split prefill into token chunks to limit decode stalls. The chunk size also sets the GPU batch width and the size of activation transfers between stages. Small chunks reload model weights more often. Large chunks can keep the GPU and the link busy long enough to delay interactive requests.
  PipeAxes runs wide prefill batches a few layers at a time so decodes can run between slices. A fused Triton Hadamard-INT4 codec compresses activations, which travel in independently sized row groups over parallel TCP sockets. The scheduler uses latency slack to choose batch width, slice depth, and row-group size. We evaluated PipeAxes in 97 replays covering 5,016 requests on A800, RTX 4090, and RTX 3090 GPUs. All 74 requests met their latency targets during a tenfold bandwidth swing. In a four-stage mixture-of-experts pipeline, PipeAxes served requests within their latency targets at 23.3x the rate of calibrated Revisit-PP and 4.44x the rate of Fixed-4096 with Express. In a mixed 64K-context workload, p95 time to first token for short requests fell from 129.8 s with native vLLM to 512 ms. With INT4 transport, MMLU accuracy rose by 0.06 percentage points and GSM8K accuracy fell by 0.46 percentage points relative to BF16.

title: Commit2Drive: Perception-Grounded Language Decisions as Commitments for Trajectory Planning in Vision-Language-Action Driving Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models introduce language reasoning into end-to-end autonomous driving. They output a language decision together with a trajectory, which makes the planner more interpretable. However, in existing methods the language decision is either an independent output or an index that selects among similar candidate trajectories, and its annotations are not verified against the trajectory. As a result, the language decision and the trajectory are often inconsistent in closed-loop driving. To address this, we propose Commit2Drive, a framework that imposes the language decision as a consistency constraint on trajectory planning. The decision is a commitment, a maneuver class with a continuous parameter that one deterministic rule reads from any trajectory, and it is grounded in facts reported by the perception of the model itself. A Maneuver Bank maps the commitment to a code with a kinematic meaning, and consistency losses train the planner to execute every admissible decision of a scene, so that the trajectory follows the decision. An automatic data pipeline supplies the supervision. Decisions are labeled from the future motion of the expert, counterfactual executions train the decision and the trajectory together, and rule-based functions with a Vision-Language Model (VLM) generate, review and refine the language annotations. The code is a lookup that involves no hidden state of the language model, so Commit2Drive is extensible to rule-based decisions, which the same planner executes without retraining. Commit2Drive uses a 0.5B language model and runs closed-loop inference online on a single consumer graphics card. On Bench2Drive, Commit2Drive reaches a Driving Score (DS) of 78.50 and a Success Rate (SR) of 55.91% with a lightweight model, which is competitive with the state of the art, and greatly reduces the language-action inconsistency. Code will be released soon.

title: Do We Really Need an LLM for Weight-Space Programming? A Deterministic Forward-Only Paradigm and Its Capability Boundaries
summary: Recent work on Weight-Space Programming uses LLMs to edit neural weights with forward passes only, conflating LLM scripting with the underlying algebra of forward-only editing. We show that for core structured editing regimes, an LLM optimizer is unnecessary, and introduce Forward Weight-Space Programming (FWSP): a deterministic pipeline combining probing, localization, stratified operators (O1-O4), automatic blind routing (83.3% vs. 33.3% for a 27B LLM with the same tool library), and paired verification with zero additional per-token computation. For reasoning LLMs, we propose Protected FisherGate, a closed-form covariance-whitened readout edit orthogonal to normal-reasoning states: on DeepSeek-R1-0528-8B, a single frozen math-calibrated patch achieves 84.2% HumanEval pass@1 (1K budget; 75.4 +/- 9.4% across 3/5 Stage-4-passing subsets), beating 512-token-reserved budget forcing by +14.6 pp (-23.4% tokens) while transferring across HF-to-vLLM backends on full GSM8K and MATH-500. Across five modalities and thirteen models (50K to 27B dense and FP8 MoE), we further prove and verify two operator boundaries, subspace entanglement and frozen representation span, where FWSP-localized LoRA bridges forward-only and gradient adaptation.

title: SEAM: A Self-Evolving and Adaptive Probing Framework for Automatic MLLM Hallucination Evaluation
summary: The severe susceptibility of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to hallucinations poses a critical threat to their reliability, making a rigorous evaluation framework indispensable. However, existing evaluation pipelines largely rely on predefined test items, suffering from high construction costs, rapid obsolescence as MLLMs evolve, and ineffectiveness in probing model-specific weaknesses. To address these limitations, we propose SEAM, a self-evolving and adaptive probing framework for automatic MLLM hallucination evaluation. Specifically, SEAM introduces a composable Hallucination Probe Construction Library comprising ten hallucination-probing skills, three elicitation wrappers, and five question formats. Building on this library, SEAM establishes a dual-loop framework. In the inner loop (adaptive probing), skill-guided visual analysis, question composition, and hierarchical quality verification are coordinated with verifier and target-response feedback to refine test items and uncover model-specific hallucinations. In the outer loop (skill evolution), a skill updater distills historical probing trajectories into localized, reusable rule updates, which undergo held-out validation and are frozen before testing. Driven by these innovative structural designs, SEAM establishes an automated and self-evolving evaluation paradigm. Experiments across four target MLLMs and ten hallucination types demonstrate that SEAM substantially outperforms representative static benchmarks, achieving an 89.2\% relative improvement in mean valid hallucination discovery rate across 12 matched comparisons.

title: Routing and Cache Retention for Multi-Turn LLM Inference: Theory and Implementation
summary: Multi-turn AI agents execute iterative loops of large language model (LLM) inference and external tool calls, transforming cluster serving into a dynamic resource-allocation problem where routing and key-value (KV) cache retention jointly govern prefix reuse across inter-turn delays. We formulate a fluid approximation of this system and show that optimal admission, routing, and eviction are governed by endpoint-specific shadow prices for computation and memory together with session continuation values. Building on this structure, we propose an asymptotically optimal buffer-reserve policy that absorbs stochastic fluctuations using a vanishing share of capacity. To handle asynchronous arrivals, delayed load reports, and engine-local memory management in production clusters, we translate these principles into a practical controller named PARK, which pairs online projected subgradient price updates and one-turn migration lookahead with a local KV retention index ranked by expected reuse value per byte-epoch. In real GPU cluster experiments serving a 197-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model on multi-turn software-engineering agent benchmarks (SWE and Terminal-Bench), PARK outperforms all five load-balancing and prefix-aware baselines across contrasting traffic regimes. On 16 H200 GPUs, PARK raises output throughput by $24.2\%$ over the strongest baseline ($336.9\%$ over round robin) on turn-intensive SWE trajectories and by $40.0\%$ over the strongest baseline ($63.3\%$ over round robin) on generation-intensive Terminal-Bench trajectories. Controlled single-replica ablations show that our retention index alone cuts prior-prefix token loss from $13.26\%$ to $2.17\%$ and increases throughput by $36.7\%$ over least-recently-used (LRU) eviction, while 128-GPU scale-up experiments sustain 50,789 to 67,363 output tokens/s across 16~replicas with prefix cache hit rates of $91.3\%$ to $97.4\%$.

title: Procedure Inference as Memory: Learning Recruiter Decision Procedures from OKF-Structured Episodes in Multi-Session Hiring Assistants
summary:
Multi-session hiring assistants must infer evolving recruiter preferences and decision patterns across projects and time. We introduce Open Knowledge Format (OKF)-indexed episodic memory to organize interactions and retrieve related events through their lineage. We also introduce Procedure Memory, which learns reusable decision procedures from these episodes through prompted reflection or reinforcement learning. We compare these approaches with no memory, full-history context, and conversation search, and evaluate Jev-class models for index navigation and GPT-5.6 Luna as a lower-cost alternative to GPT-5.4.
  In our evaluation, OKF-indexed retrieval achieves low-priority preference F1 scores of 0.93-0.95 at medium and high preference overlap between hiring projects. It significantly outperforms full-history context and conversation search in both settings, and no memory at high overlap, while using 69% fewer context tokens than full history. Procedure Memory reduces conversational turns by up to 39% relative to no memory. Qualitative and long-horizon evaluations provide evidence of temporal reasoning, with RL-learned procedures achieving 60% on both correct abstention and exact-field identification. Jev-class models improve conversational efficiency but more frequently miss temporally relevant evidence, highlighting the importance of evidence selection.
  On PersonaMem-v2, Procedure Memory with OKF retrieval achieves 50.2% accuracy versus 48.6% for full-history context and 29.0% for no memory, using 90.5% fewer reader input tokens than full history. GPT-5.6 Luna performs comparably to GPT-5.4 at lower cost. These findings highlight the value of structured episodic memory and learned decision procedures for efficient personalization and temporal reasoning.

title: Sage-Med: Scaling Medical Multimodal Intelligence
summary: Establishing effective scaling laws for medical multimodal large language models (MLLMs) remains a persistent and fundamental challenge. Our systematic evaluation shows that existing medical MLLMs tend to underperform frontier general-purpose MLLMs across a range of medical tasks, while scaling model size primarily improves text capabilities rather than multimodal perception, and enabling reasoning modes fails to close this visual gap. To investigate how medical multimodal intelligence scales in practice, we introduce Sage-Med-Preview, a 35B-parameter medical multimodal model with 3B activated parameters, built by combining stage-specific curation over 322.7 million candidate records with a progressive training curriculum spanning medical pretraining, staged supervised fine-tuning, and adaptive reinforcement learning. Across this curriculum, progressive supervised refinement and adaptive reinforcement learning yield consistent stage-wise gains, substantially advancing both specialized visual understanding and medical language capabilities. Evaluated against 77 competing models across 238 clinical tasks spanning 61 public and 13 private multi-center benchmarks in more than 40 modalities, Sage-Med-Preview achieves an average score of 58.26% on the 31 public multimodal benchmarks. It outperforms the state-of-the-art open-source medical model Hulu-Med-235B-A22B at 50.99% and the general scientific model Intern-S2-Preview at 52.24%, and approaches the advanced proprietary model GPT-6.2-Sol across multiple tasks such as comprehensive multimodal understanding, report generation, and visual grounding. Although substantial challenges remain in complex medical reasoning and multi-step clinical workflows, this report provides empirical evidence, actionable data and training recipes, and a rigorous benchmark toward scalable clinical multimodal intelligence.

title: M$^{2}$AdaptVLA: Multimodal Memory-Augmented Vision-Language-Action Model with Predictive Test-Time Adaptation
summary: Effective robotic manipulation calls for multimodal memory and rapid adaptation to shifts in contact dynamics. However, many existing policies, which retain either visual or wrench history, may miss key cues from the other modality. Moreover, even with wrench memory, fixed policies can struggle when contact conditions shift at deployment. To this end, we introduce M$^{2}$AdaptVLA, a vision-language-action model that integrates visual and wrench memories with predictive test-time adaptation. For visual memory, the model uses test-time training (TTT) to encode observation history in fast weights. Each entry in the bounded TTT bank combines the corresponding frame's features with a readout from these weights, preserving cues that predate the oldest retained frame. For wrench memory, a context gate controls how much the action expert draws on wrench history as it jointly denoises future actions and wrenches. For predictive test-time adaptation, the auxiliary wrench prediction loss also provides online self-supervision. Using measured wrenches as targets, we update low-rank policy adapters by backpropagating only through the final denoising step. Real-world experiments show that the TTT bank outperforms visual memory baselines on progress tracking, scene recall, and demonstration following. On contact-sensitive tasks, the context gate yields higher success rates than direct injection or gated cross-attention. Predictive test-time adaptation improves robustness to shifts in contact dynamics. On eight tasks requiring visual and wrench memory, M$^{2}$AdaptVLA achieves a mean success rate of 82.71%, a 31.46% absolute gain over the strongest baseline. The project page is available at https://tlf-tlf.github.io/M2AdaptVLAPage/.

title: SCO-Hyper-Meta-Double-GroupNN: A Double-Group SU(2) Hyper-/Meta-Graph Neural Network for Cooperative Spin-Crossover Potential Energy Surfaces
summary: Learning potential energy surfaces for magnetic materials requires resolving coupled local spin manifolds and geometric frustration. We introduce SCO-Hyper-Meta-Double-GroupNN, a geometry-only architecture combining a pretrained O(3)-equivariant backbone with SU(2) spinor Hamiltonians and cooperative hyper-/meta-graph interactions. Analytic thermal spinor density matrices provide non-polynomial two- and three-body structural invariants, while frustrated-triangle hyperedges and a multi-shell sideway gate couple geometric representations to local spin manifolds. A variationally consistent, doubly-centered zero-gauge free-energy functional couples multiplet occupations and signed spin orientations, yielding conservative autograd forces without spin inputs at inference. On a first-principles Co-Cr-Ni benchmark comprising 346 training and 59 held-out validation supercells across crystalline, amorphous, glassy, and liquid regimes, compact models with 56k-77k parameters outperform a 207k-parameter spin-conditioned magnetic MACE baseline. Energy MAE decreases by 37-44%, reaching 3.82 versus 6.83 meV/atom, and force MAE decreases by 10.8-14.2 meV/Angstrom, reaching 165.8-169.2 versus 180.0 meV/Angstrom. The models preserve Kramers degeneracy to within $6\times10^{-15}$ eV, predict equilibrium local magnetic moments from geometry alone with an absolute-moment MAE of $0.181\,μ_B$, and support stable molecular dynamics up to 2,200 K. This framework integrates local spinor symmetry and cooperative magnetic interactions into geometry-only interatomic potentials.

title: HAS: Hierarchical Adaptive Frame Sampling for Video Understanding
summary: Due to context-length constraints, most MLLMs cannot process full-length videos and therefore rely on sampling a subset of frames as input. However, existing sampling methods, ranging from uniform sampling to relevance-based selection, are often driven by a single sampling principle and thus struggle to accommodate the heterogeneous evidential requirements of different queries: some demand a holistic understanding of how the video unfolds over time, while others hinge on fine-grained events within a short temporal window. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{Hierarchical Adaptive Frame Sampling (HAS)}, a two-stage frame sampling framework. In the first stage, \emph{Backbone Frame Construction}, we apply a Determinantal Point Process (DPP) to sample frames that are both query-relevant and non-redundant. These selected frames capture key moments across the video and form the backbone of the sampling set, providing a foundation for subsequent enrichment. In the second stage, \emph{Adaptive Contextual Enrichment}, we analyze the temporal distribution of the backbone frames to infer the query's requirements and adaptively allocate the remaining frame budget between Local and Global Context. The Local Context enriches the backbone with fine-grained temporal dynamics and short-range causal relations, whereas the Global Context connects temporally isolated evidence and provides a holistic view of the entire video to support global understanding. Through such a hierarchical two-stage process, HAS effectively addresses diverse query requirements. Incorporated into three leading MLLMs, it demonstrates consistently superior performance across the Video-MME, LongVideoBench, and MLVU benchmarks.

title: EPPC-CARE: Staged Hierarchical Annotation of Communication Behaviors in Secure Patient-Provider Messages
summary: Objectives: Patient portal messages provide invaluable information about communication dynamics between patients and healthcare providers, but extracting it manually is labor-intensive. We developed and evaluated EPPC-CARE, an automated framework for identifying communication behaviors together with the supporting text for each classification. Materials and Methods: From 867 messages, we obtained 5,516 reference standard annotations. Each annotation is a triplet of communication-related text (span), a broader communication category (Code), and a specific subcategory (Sub-code). We evaluated EPPC-CARE's identified triplets across six open-weight large language models (LLMs) against supervised fine-tuning and communication-based models such as EPPC-OASIS. We also compared EPPC-CARE with human expert annotations on 100 messages. Results: EPPC-CARE improved performance over EPPC-OASIS across all six models. EPPC-CARE's Triplet F1 improved by 2.90 percentage points on average, with a best score of 64.4%. On the human expert evaluation subset, EPPC-CARE and the human expert showed comparable agreement with the reference standard, with differences favoring EPPC-CARE. Discussion: These findings suggest that identifying triplet components (span, code, subcode) sequentially can improve performance across model families while preserving the supporting text behind each identification. EPPC-CARE links the communication code and subcode with the source text (span), supporting human verification of automated annotations in clinical informatics. EPPC-CARE may therefore make larger-scale studies of patient-provider communication more feasible and provide a foundation for human-in-the-loop annotation workflows. Conclusion: EPPC-CARE offers a more reliable and reviewable approach for automated characterization of communication behaviors in secure patient-provider messaging.

title: Dynamic Task Update Benchmark (DTU-Bench): Evaluating Runtime Task Adaptation in Robotic Manipulation
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies perform well on fixed-instruction robotic manipulation benchmarks, but their ability to adapt to instruction changes during execution remains understudied. We introduce the Dynamic Task Update Benchmark (DTU-Bench), evaluating 40 task revisions across seven update types and three execution stages using LIBERO, a simulated robotic manipulation benchmark. We compare performance when a new instruction is given before execution starts versus during execution, and examine whether the new task instructions are followed. Across 13 representative VLA configurations, average task success is 95.8% on the original object-manipulation tasks, compared with only 1.6% when the instruction changes which object to manipulate during execution. Controlled diagnostics show that policies often complete the original task before the updated one, and that their responses depend on the robot's physical state. We further test whether a simple scripted controller that releases the grasped object and moves the arm back helps robots respond to instruction changes. This improves success from 2% to 38% for π0.5 and from 8% to 48% for DM0.5, but can cause unwanted object motion. These findings reveal limitations that fixed-instruction benchmarks and task-success metrics alone can overlook in evaluating robotic manipulation. Project page: https://dtu-bench.github.io/

title: Kant-Q: A Q-Learning Algorithm for Kantian Equilibrium in Symmetric Markov Games
summary: AI agents increasingly interact with one another, and many of these interactions are mixed-motive games, which have posed a persistent challenge for learning algorithms. Most multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) algorithms are designed to reach Nash equilibria, yet in many such games these equilibria are Pareto-inefficient. We instead study Kantian equilibria, an economic solution concept in which each agent plays the action it would want all agents to adopt. In symmetric games, this corresponds to an optimal common policy. We propose Kant-Q, a Q-learning algorithm in which each agent learns action profiles where all agents play the same action. Each update is then a sample from a single-agent MDP, so Kant-Q inherits the convergence guarantees of standard Q-learning. We show that every symmetric Markov game has a pure Kantian equilibrium. We also prove that all agents' Q-tables converge to the same limit, whose greedy policy is such an equilibrium, and that greedy play converges whenever the optimal common action is unique at every state. We further show that in a subclass of symmetric monotone games, the Kantian equilibrium is Pareto-efficient among pure strategy profiles and strictly individually rational. Empirically, on the iterated Prisoner's Dilemma and the GovSim fishery with up to 200 agents, Kant-Q learns the Kantian equilibrium, while the baselines underperform. Since copies of the same AI system naturally face one another in symmetric games, these results suggest universalization as a design principle for cooperative AI-AI interaction.

title: AliceAI-Foundation-80B-A3B-Base
summary: We present AliceAI-Foundation-80B-A3B-Base, a mixture-of-experts language model with 80 billion total parameters and approximately 3 billion active parameters per token, trained from scratch at Yandex and released under the Apache 2.0 license. The model combines Kimi Delta Attention with full attention, uses Attention Residuals, and is trained with Muon. Training comprises general pretraining on 17.5 trillion tokens, two context-extension stages, and a dedicated stage for reasoning and agentic interaction. We describe the data collection and augmentation pipelines, evaluation protocols, architectural ablations, and scaling-law experiments. We identify the limitations of held-out training loss as a proxy for downstream performance and introduce an auxiliary loss on mixture-of-experts outputs to stabilize training at the predicted learning rate. Domain-specific data selection and augmentation improve factual knowledge, mathematics, and programming skills, while agent trajectories introduced during pretraining improve performance on agentic benchmarks after supervised fine-tuning. In zero-shot reasoning evaluation, the model achieves leading results among open base models of comparable size, with 88.7% pass@8 on IMO-AnswerBench and 82.9% pass@8 on LiveCodeBench v5-v6. To evaluate Russian-language factual knowledge, we introduce and release two benchmarks with their evaluation protocols: WikiWebFacts, which tests short factual questions drawn from encyclopedic sources and search queries, and HardMultiQA, which tests more demanding factual questions inspired by user interactions. Our model scores 86.5% on WikiWebFacts and 67.9% on HardMultiQA, compared with 83.2% and 65.4% for DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base (284B total and 13B active parameters) and 72.8% and 54.5% for Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B-Base (120B total and 12B active parameters), outperforming both larger models on these benchmarks.

title: Resilience Analysis Through Automated Stage Identification and Quantitative Assessment
summary: This paper introduced an ML-based approach, designed to be domain- and threat-agnostic, for automated recognition of PARA (Plan/Prepare, Absorb, Recover, Adapt) resilience stages in system-performance time series, enabling subsequent quantitative resilience analysis across different systems. We investigate four ML models for resilience stage recognition: Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost). We then use the ML models' predictions to quantify system resilience by computing corresponding resilience metrics from system-performance data observed before, during, and after disruptive events. We evaluate the proposed approach using datasets from two distinct operational domain network systems and an airport transportation system, demonstrating its domain-agnostic applicability to resilience assessment. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of resilience stage classification, with the best F1-scores ranging from 74.3% to 99.4% across all resilience stages. The overall resilience metrics R_t and RL are estimated, with the best models' MAPE ranging from 0.35-0.82% on IEEE 802.11 and LTE to 1.65-9.56% for the airport. These results provide a basis for threat-agnostic resilience analysis of complex engineering systems, enabling further assessment of how effectively a system withstands, absorbs, and recovers from disruptive events and stress conditions.

title: PURA: Video Token Pruning via Unified Spatiotemporal Redundancy Assessment
summary: Video large language models incur substantial inference costs from long visual token sequences. Existing video token compression methods mitigate these costs by exploiting spatial redundancy within frames and temporal redundancy across frames. However, many approaches impose predefined processing orders or fixed allocation ratios for spatial and temporal compression, limiting their ability to adapt to the varying balance of spatiotemporal redundancy across videos. To address this limitation, we propose PURA, a training-free method that prunes visual tokens through unified spatiotemporal redundancy assessment. For each token, PURA constructs spatial and temporal reference candidates and selects the reference with the lowest representation error across the two dimensions. The representation error is combined with token importance to determine each token's removal cost. To avoid the time overhead of removing the lowest-cost token one by one, we introduce Coordinated Pruning, which iteratively groups mutually compatible low-cost removals into batches for simultaneous execution and updates the pruning state after each batch until the target budget is reached. Extensive experiments on three video large language models and five video understanding benchmarks demonstrate that PURA achieves a favorable trade-off between task performance and inference efficiency.

title: Feasibility-Aware Deep Reinforcement Learning for O-CU and O-DU Mapping in 6G O-RAN
summary: This paper studies the mapping of the virtual network function components (VNFCs) of the O-RAN central unit (O-CU) and O-RAN distributed unit (O-DU) onto virtual machines (VMs) in sixth-generation (6G) open radio access networks (O-RAN). The problem is formulated as a feasibility-aware sequential decision process that maximizes the number of placed VNFCs and, secondarily, favors fewer active VMs and lower residual resource wastage. Although conventional optimization techniques can solve this problem, their computational cost becomes prohibitive for larger instances or when optimization must be repeated. To address this limitation, we explore two neural reinforcement learning (RL)-based methods: a deep $Q$-network (DQN) and a double deep $Q$-network (Double DQN). Whereas DQN uses the same target network to both select and evaluate the bootstrap action, Double DQN decouples these two operations to mitigate maximization-induced overestimation. We compare both methods against six baselines: random feasible placement, first-fit, first-fit decreasing, best-fit, a resource-wastage-aware heuristic, and a time-bounded mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) solver. We conduct a controlled experimental evaluation across four problem sizes with $30$ independent instances each, together with capacity-stress, distribution-shift, and reward-ablation experiments. For the $16 \times 8$ VNFC-to-VM scenario, DQN and Double DQN achieve mean placed-VNFC fractions of $0.990$ and $0.996$, respectively. However, first-fit decreasing and the resource-wastage-aware heuristic match this placement quality with lower efficiency cost and lower decision time, whereas the MILP attains the lowest efficiency cost at a much higher runtime. The results clarify the strengths and limitations of neural placement for this static problem, without establishing superiority over conventional methods.

title: Decoder-as-a-Probe: Verbalizing and Steering Visual Representations in LVLMs
summary: It is commonly accepted that high-level concepts are represented linearly in the representation space of large neural networks. For Large Vision Language Models (LVLMs), finding those interpretable directions in visual representations is important for interpretability. To find them, the classical approach is to train a linear classifier on the representations, but it needs a large amount of labels and only recovers what can be read from the representations, not what the model actually uses. In this paper we start from the following insight: The LLM Decoder of an LVLM is also a classifier whose classes are the possible next tokens. So we use its first-order Taylor expansion as a linear classifier. Hence, we introduce Decoder-as-a-Probe (DaP), which significantly outperforms classical probing and steering baselines especially when training data is sparse. (1) It verbalizes what an LVLM perceives in a given image. (2) It can surgically change the perception of the LVLM about specific attributes (e.g. change only the color, the clothes worn or the action done). Due to its simplicity and data efficiency, we believe DaP can serve as a plug-and-play tool for LVLM research, such as interpretability, hallucination mitigation or instruction tuning.

title: Know the Design, Pick the Attack: Sentence-Keyed Watermarks for LLMs
summary: A watermark lets the provider of a language model recognise the text its model wrote, which matters more as generated text becomes hard to tell from human writing: provenance underpins academic integrity, the fight against misinformation and new regulation. Providers have started to watermark the text of their models, and to explain how their watermarks work. Explaining a watermark, however, also tells an attacker how to break it, and there are two ways to do so: reword the text to erase the mark, or learn the mark and copy it onto text the model never wrote. Each attack has been studied on its own. We study an attacker that reads the published design to choose between them: it erases the watermarks that are hard to learn and forges the ones that survive rewording. Against it, every existing watermark we compare fails. We propose KeyedLex, which reads its secret key from the grammar of the previous sentence, which rewording changes little, and whose detector does not need to recover the key exactly. It outperforms every watermark we compare on both models we test, losing about half of its signal where the best alternative loses two thirds, at no extra cost in text quality over the best-known watermarks.

title: DiversePlace: Diversity-Seeking Curriculum Reinforcement Learning for Macro Placement
summary: Macro placement is a critical early-stage decision in physical design because macro locations strongly constrain subsequent implementation stages. The task is difficult because these high-impact discrete decisions must be made before downstream quality can be measured accurately, forcing training to rely on fast but imperfect training-time oracles such as half-perimeter wirelength (HPWL). Existing RL-based placers therefore mostly optimize single HPWL-driven solutions, and their long sequential horizons often require heavy search assistance or offline expert data while leaving little room to preserve multiple competitive layouts. We address this gap by making quality-controlled diversity an explicit objective for macro placement. Instead of relying on a single proxy-optimal solution, we maintain a compact archive of HPWL-competitive yet meaningfully different placements for downstream selection. We realize this idea in DiversePlace, a curriculum proximal policy optimization (PPO) framework that combines a quality-gated diversity reward with an expanding placement horizon, enabling from-scratch RL optimization while keeping exploration inside competitive HPWL regions. On the ISPD2005 benchmarks, DiversePlace consistently improves top-5, top-10, and top-20 archive diversity and achieves lower or virtually identical HPWL on all eight designs with better efficiency. Code: https://github.com/William030422/NIPS2026-DiversePlace.

title: Evidence-Aligned Benchmarking and Learning for Medical Video Language Models
summary: A medical video language model should answer from the visual evidence its question asks about. We find three places where this breaks down and address each with an approach we call MedEvidU. First, benchmarks reward answers that ignore the video: on one dataset, the position of a clip within its recording predicts the surgical step in 37% of questions, and a constant answer beats every trained model on a standard safety-assessment metric. We build MedVidBench-v2, 34 tasks from 18 surgical and clinical video datasets, in which prompts and metrics are audited with answers given without video, and which tests unseen hospitals and windows cut blindly from whole recordings. Second, common video encoders merge consecutive frames into shared tokens, so a question about one frame is answered from a blend of two. Query-slot inputs give each queried frame its own tokens at almost no extra cost. Third, a fine-tuned model has memorized its training questions, which leaves little to learn from. Label-matched question resampling (LQR) adds unseen questions about the same recordings while keeping the answer distribution fixed, in a final supervised epoch and in reinforcement learning. Together, these raise the grounding IoU of a 4B model from 30.4 to 44.4, above a supervised 27B model, and instrument grounding at an unseen hospital from 33.9 to 72.5. On blindly cut windows, event-presence accuracy improves by 5.5 points and localization F1 by 8.1 points. Project page: https://gaozhongpai.github.io/MedEvidU/

title: HoloBrain-0.5 Technical Report
summary:
We present HoloBrain-0.5, a family of vision-language-action (VLA) models for manipulation across robot embodiments. The policies plan in a shared action space using robot state, kinematic structure, and calibrated camera observations. We standardize joint axes, coordinate frames, and tool-center points in robot descriptions (URDFs) and encode their kinematic graphs in a shared 3D representation. HoloBrain-0.5-Continuous generates action chunks by diffusion, while HoloBrain-0.5-Discrete uses residual finite scalar quantization (FSQ) and delayed autoregression. We pretrain both policies on over 10,000 hours of real-robot, simulation, and human-manipulation data spanning 15 embodiment categories.
  Across six closed-loop simulation settings, the discrete policy converges faster and reaches a higher mean success rate than the continuous policy (56.77% vs. 49.71%). On seven real-robot tasks, it achieves a mean progress score of 87.76% without task-specific post-training. After post-training, the continuous policy outperforms $π_{0.5}$ on the seven-task benchmark (94.52% vs. 86.25%) and an 11-task dual-arm benchmark (79.07% vs. 69.41%). The discrete-initialized continuous policy transfers five tasks zero-shot from Piper to Piper-X, scoring 63.28% on average. With target-robot demonstrations, the continuous policy scores 89.2% on Franka Panda and 92.94% on a mobile dual-arm platform. Although pretraining includes no Unitree G1 data, post-training with limited G1 demonstrations yields a mean progress score of 70.24% across three humanoid tasks, compared with 11.00% for $π_{0.5}$.

title: PreserveReward: Reliable Consistency Reward Modeling for Image Editing via Dual-Teacher On-Policy Self-Distillation
summary: Instruction-guided image editing has a wide range of applications, yet existing models may inadvertently alter content that should remain unchanged. Reliable consistency evaluation is therefore essential for assessing content preservation and providing reward signals for Reinforcement Learning (RL). However, existing reward models may overlook subtle visual changes or fail to distinguish necessary modifications from unintended alterations, limiting the reliability of consistency assessment. To address this challenge, we propose PreserveReward, a consistency reward model for image editing that integrates visual On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) to enhance fine-grained visual perception and consistency assessment. PreserveReward learns from reference preservation scores through a regression-based scoring loss and employs two complementary teacher views for self-distillation. The local teacher uses matched crops to identify subtle visual changes, while the joint teacher combines local details with global context to determine whether these changes align with the editing intent. To improve the reliability of distillation supervision, we calibrate teacher score distributions via minimum-KL projection under reference-score error constraints and adaptively select teacher process supervision based on gradient alignment with the scoring objective, mitigating scoring bias and optimization conflicts. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that PreserveReward achieves strong alignment with human preference on non-edited content preservation and generalizes well across diverse editing scenarios.

title: vSFT: Learning to Verbally Tune Agents at Test Time
summary: Large language model agents are increasingly improved via agentic reinforcement learning, which can be on-policy but suffers from expensive rollouts and sparse rewards, limiting its application at test time. In this paper, we present a verbally Supervised Fine-Tuning (vSFT) framework that enables the conjunction of dense feedback in natural language and weight updates at test time. Specifically, our vSFT forms a closed loop between an agent and a supervisor via a hypernetwork, in which the supervisor generates verbal supervision from the agent's failed trajectories, and the hypernetwork converts that supervision into low-rank weight updates to tune the agent. We validate that this test-time in-parameter evolving process outperforms both its in-context counterparts and prevalent reinforcement learning methods. In particular, our vSFT using Qwen3-4B outperforms GRPO and Reflexion by 8.7% and 13.9% in success rate on ALFWorld, and by 4.8% and 18.2% on WebShop, respectively. We believe that learning how to adapt a model, rather than an adapted model, offers a promising path towards more capable agents that improve themselves.

title: Grounding User Preferences in Shared Multimodal Concepts for Recommendation
summary: Multimodal recommendation has substantially advanced item understanding by incorporating rich visual and textual content. Yet user preferences are still commonly encoded as implicit signals tied to individual items, leaving recurring semantic factors without persistent identities that can be shared across items. We introduce MKGE, a multimodal knowledge graph framework that represents these factors as canonical, addressable concepts. MKGE induces a domain-adaptive concept vocabulary from item images and titles, grounds each user's interaction history in supported concepts, and jointly models direct user-item evidence and concept-mediated preference signals. By turning recurring semantics into shared coordinates, MKGE enables evidence from different items to accumulate around the same preference factors. Extensive experiments on three public benchmarks demonstrate that MKGE consistently outperforms collaborative, knowledge-graph, multimodal, and recent LLM/MLLM-based recommenders across all six reported metrics. Controlled studies further demonstrate the importance of canonical concept identities and personalized user-concept correspondence, with especially pronounced gains over removing or rewiring the user graph for low-activity users. These results establish canonical multimodal concepts as effective units for preference modeling and transfer. Code, constructed knowledge graphs, and prompts are available at https://github.com/Garden1a-X/MKGE.

title: Most of the Way There: Turning a Strong Video Prior into an Action-Conditioned World Model
summary: Modern video generators excel at producing visually plausible futures guided by text and image prompts. Yet their emphasis on semantic plausibility does not guarantee fidelity to the physical consequences of specific actions. Action-conditioned world models (ACWMs), in contrast, aim to simulate how the world responds to robot actions, enabling scalable policy evaluation and improvement without costly real-world rollouts. The challenge is not merely to generate a plausible future, but to predict what follows from a specific physical action. As video priors grow stronger, we ask how little adaptation is truly needed to bridge this gap. We introduce Dianjing, a minimal recipe that preserves and unlocks the capabilities of strong video priors through unified physical action conditioning, training concentrated at the high noise levels where motion and layout, and thus the consequences of actions, are decided, and native history conditioning. Built upon MiniMax H3, a 33B video foundation model, Dianjing freezes the pretrained backbone and trains only 0.34% of its parameters using approximately 65 hours of robot video across two embodiments, without additional robot-specific pretraining or camera calibration. Controlled ablations show that where training is allocated across noise levels matters more than how actions enter the network. On WorldOracle, which evaluates predictions against paired real-world executions, Dianjing achieves the best scores on four of the five evaluation tracks and ranks second on AgiBot-Long. Our findings suggest that strong video priors already bring us most of the way to world modeling; lightweight physical action grounding can unlock their potential for real-world prediction.

title: Mitigating Hallucinations in Medical Question Answering on ESC Cardiology Guidelines: Evaluation and Retrieval Optimization
summary: Background: Large language models produce hallucinations in medical question answering (QA). Verify-and-revise pipelines that check atomic claims against retrieved guideline evidence are a standard mitigation, but evaluations almost universally treat the verifier's output as ground truth, an assumption rarely tested. Objective: To measure, claim by claim against human judgement, how such a pipeline fails in a guideline-grounded clinical setting. Methods: We built a dataset of 160 questions (100 patient vignettes from 89 de-identified cases, 60 fact-based) over four recent ESC cardiology guidelines, all approved by a practising internist, and a retrieval corpus of 627 hand-verified guideline records at two chunk granularities. A five-stage pipeline was run under four retrieval configurations and three independent runs (1920 arm-runs); all 606 first-pass refuted claims were manually audited, an independent judge re-judged 906 decisions, and the expert blindly reviewed 100 accepted claims. Results: Only 44.7-50.6% of flagged claims were true hallucinations. Correction loops converged in 85.2-95.1% of cases, yet 35% of genuine final errors were introduced by correction. Single-run true-hallucination recall was 35.6-41.2%, the three-run union 71-80%; verifier agreement was moderate (kappa = 0.505). The blind probe estimated the accepted-claim miss rate at 3.2% (95% CI 0.7-6.7%). Final genuine-error rate: 1.7% of answers. Conclusion: Claim-level verification reduces hallucinated content by an order of magnitude, but verifier reliability, not generation, is the limiting factor and must be measured, not assumed.

title: Can Visual World Models See Force?
summary: World models and vision-language-action policy models are increasingly proposed as foundations for robot manipulation. They predict how scenes evolve and which actions to take, yet successful manipulation depends not solely on following observable trajectories but also on the hidden variable of interaction force. Neurophysiology has shown that humans possess a visual prior for this hidden variable, motivating us to ask the question: Do the representations of visual foundation models also capture the forces involved in an interaction? We define force awareness as the ability of representations to (1) indicate when contact force is applied, (2) track how it changes during an interaction, and (3) reflect how large it is. We probe frozen image, video, world- and policy model representations with a lightweight readout trained on synchronized video and force measurements from two manipulation datasets. Our experiments show that most models capture when contact occurs but not how much force is being applied. Surprisingly, robot post-training does not improve this either, highlighting an important gap in current models capabilities.

title: DocSEAM: Bidirectional Cross-Page Encoding for Multi-Page Document Understanding
summary: Multi-page document vision-language models encode each page independently, creating a feature-level discontinuity at page boundaries: visual tokens are formed without access to content on adjacent pages, and the language model must reason over these page representations formed in isolation. We introduce DocSEAM (Document Selective Enrichment via Anchored Masking), a lightweight module inserted between a pretrained vision encoder and the language model that injects the inductive bias of local cross-page context into visual representations. For each page, DocSEAM forms a local triplet with its two neighbors, applies center-anchored masked self-attention with directional salience gates to fuse information from neighbor pages, and returns only the enriched center-page tokens, leaving the visual token count unchanged. After a supervised cross-page warm-up and multi-page fine-tuning with DocSEAM frozen, our 9B-parameter model achieves state-of-the-art results among the evaluated open-weight models of up to 10B parameters on five multi-page document VQA benchmarks. We further show that under controlled re-pagination, DocSEAM reduces sensitivity to boundary placement and improves cross-page span localization

title: Any-Rate: Half-Bit Multi-Precision LLM Quantization with Coded Bit-Planes
summary: Nested multi-precision quantization derives multiple precisions from a single checkpoint by reading only the leading bits of each weight, which makes it attractive for on-device deployment under varying memory and energy budgets. However, existing methods offer only integer bits, leaving large accuracy gaps between adjacent precisions and severe degradation at 2 bits. To address this, we propose Any-Rate, which serves 2-8 bits from one checkpoint, in half-bit steps over 2-4 bits. Any-Rate restricts some bit-planes to extended Hamming codewords in 8-weight blocks (0.5 bits per weight), shares one LUT per row across precisions, and encodes all precisions jointly with a separate target for each, reducing the loss from sharing bit-planes. Across four LLMs, Any-Rate achieves state-of-the-art accuracy among multi-precision methods at 2 and 3 bits, keeping 69% of FP16 accuracy at 2 bits, and is within one point of the best at 4 bits. It decodes about as fast as existing kernels, and an LPDDR energy model estimates up to 27% less energy at equal accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/hoonki2002/Any-Rate.

title: EvoLink-Bench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Self-Evolving Agents in Long-Horizon Interdependent Task Streams
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are evolving from passive chatbots into autonomous systems that operate continuously in dynamic environments. Such agents need not only solve current tasks but also learn from past interactions to improve future performance. However, existing streaming benchmarks often rely on short task sequences or largely independent tasks, providing limited evidence of whether agents can effectively reuse experience when later tasks depend on earlier outcomes. To address this gap, we introduce \textbf{EvoLink-Bench}, a benchmark for evaluating self-evolving agents in long-horizon, interdependent task streams. It covers daily office work, multi-turn dialogue, and AutoResearch-style workflows, with persistent workspaces and dependencies across tasks. The benchmark includes two complementary levels: \textbf{L1}, which evaluates the acquisition and revision of language-expressible knowledge, and \textbf{L2}, which assesses the development of task-level capabilities through execution and feedback. Its evaluation further distinguishes within-task recovery, persistent-state updates, and experience reuse in later tasks. We evaluate five agent frameworks across three backbone configurations under three persistence conditions, covering 19,635 scored task slots from selected evaluation cohorts. Results show that no framework consistently performs best across both levels, retries recover only a limited proportion of failed tasks, and persistent-state updates do not necessarily improve subsequent performance. Furthermore, the effects of evolution differ between knowledge- and capability-level tasks, suggesting that these two forms of evolution require different learning mechanisms. Performance gains also vary across domains and task streams, with improvements on some tasks not necessarily extending to others.

title: Towards Democratized Academic LLM Hosting: Practical insights from needs, implementations, and governance across Dutch institutions
summary: Academic LLM hosting is emerging as an operational infrastructure domain with recurring socio-technical patterns, tensions, and governance requirements across institutions. Based on a workshop with academic infrastructure, research-support, education, and policy-adjacent stakeholders, this paper synthesizes current practices and open questions around institutionally governed LLM services for Dutch academia. It highlights challenges around deployment models, energy and utilization, governance, tooling, commercial integration, and research and education use cases, and identifies emerging directions for service pathways, coordination, and responsible operation.
authors: the Towards Democratized Academic LLM Hosting Workshop Consortium

title: AgentLens: Graph-guided Security Auditing for LLM-based Agents
summary: LLM-based agents are emerging as a key paradigm for automating software engineering by coupling LLM-driven decision-making with external tools, files, APIs, and execution environments. However, weaknesses in agent implementations and insecure interactions between the agent and external resources can lead to severe consequences, including remote code execution, arbitrary file access, SQL injection, and data leakage. This makes pre-deployment auditing essential for systematically identifying implementation weaknesses and validating whether they can manifest as concrete security risks in realistic agent workflows. Existing approaches either focus on specific vulnerability classes or lack the capability to validate whether identified static weaknesses correspond to executable exploits. In this paper, we propose AgentLens, a systematic auditing framework for LLM-based agents. AgentLens analyzes the target agent's implementation, component interactions, and built-in defenses, and organizes them into an Audit Knowledge Graph that captures how these factors interact to expose potential security risks. Based on this graph, AgentLens derives candidate attack paths, generates path-specific validation payloads, and constructs realistic multi-turn audit scenarios that place these payloads in task-relevant contexts to validate whether suspected risks manifest as security-violating behaviors during execution. Across five widely-used agent applications, each with over 24,000 GitHub stars, AgentLens identifies 44 vulnerabilities, and every vulnerability is validated by being triggered during execution. Compared with the state-of-the-art approach (AgentFuzz), AgentLens detects 3.67$\times$ more vulnerabilities. To date, 12 reported issues have been assigned CVE IDs.

title: Under the Influence -- of What? A Controlled Evaluation of Influence Functions
summary: Influence functions are a promising way to identify which training examples are responsible for a model's output. However, so far empirical evaluations on LLM pretraining level only assumed that they work as intended. This is the first work to systematically evaluate whether the 'influential' examples actually have properties relevant to a language model output, based on re-training with controlled data splits. We investigate three prominent Hessian approximation methods (GradSim, TrackStar, K-FAC) in two settings (linguistic phenomena and factual knowledge) in GPT-2 type models (68M-5.6B training tokens). We find that on average, the `influential' examples are indeed relevant, but they do not always bear the target properties directly, and the ratio and kind of relevance varies by setting.

title: ConTra: A Training Framework for Effective Contextual Retrieval via Prefix Generation
summary: Data management systems organize large text collections for tasks such as finding relevant studies and extracting contract clauses. Systems make long documents searchable by splitting them into independently indexed chunks. Chunking can separate text from its identifying details. The indexing challenge is to keep each chunk independently searchable while preserving the context needed to find and rank it. Existing methods either encode that context in chunk vectors or attach it as a text prefix. Context encoded only in vectors is unavailable to text rerankers. Prompted prefixes serve both vector search and reranking, but are costly to generate at indexing time and can underperform contextual encoders. We propose ConTra (Context That Travels), a reinforcement learning framework for training lightweight prefix generators. Its reward combines feedback from frozen embedding and reranking models with factual verification and length control. ConTra generates one prefix per chunk during index construction and stores the augmented text and its embedding for reuse across queries. To evaluate contextual retrieval across workloads and under interference, we introduce RealContextBench, a benchmark with five application collections and three controlled conditions that isolate the effect of distracting text. On ConTEB and RealContextBench, ConTra-2B outperforms the prompted 9B baseline using Anthropic's method and the PPLX-4B contextual encoder, with a margin of up to 3.15 points over their best overall scores, while indexing short documents 7.74 times and 2.15 times as fast as those baselines, respectively. Post-trained only on ConTEB, it leads the standalone methods on RealContextBench after reranking and is less sensitive than the prompted 2B baseline to random and topically similar distractors. Code, datasets, and trained models are available at https://github.com/SStan1/ConTra.

title: Single-Database Rewards Are Hackable: Counterfactual Execution for Trustworthy Text-to-SQL RL
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) for text-to-SQL agents pays a query when its result matches the reference on one database. However, a wrong query can match by luck when the data lack the rows that expose its bug. We study a counterfactual-database (CF) reward that also runs the final query on a few hidden, code-generated copies of the database and pays only if all results match (strict form) or by the share matched (mean form). On 1,302 synthetic audit questions, the strict form lowers the share of buggy queries paid in full from 29.5% to 16.8% and of reward hacks from 54.1% to 1.9%, rejecting 0 of 2,847 correct queries; copies from a family-blind generator do about as well. In a controlled GRPO comparison on a 3.35B model with three seeds per arm, training on the mean form did not improve in-domain accuracy (8.4% vs 11.7%), because the two rewards disagreed on only 5-7% of rollouts; on Spider it gained 1.6 points. One seed reverses both signs, so single-seed reward comparisons mislead. Code: https://github.com/RishiiGamer2201/counterfactual-sql-rewards ; data, models, demo: https://huggingface.co/counterfactual-sql

title: One Patch, Many Policies: Object-Associated Physical Patch Attacks on Robotic Manipulation
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) and World Action Models (WAMs) are vulnerable to adversarial visual interference, motivating the study of universal and transferable physical patch attacks. We propose Object-Associated Patch Attack (OAPA), a universal and transferable physical patch framework that enables an attacker to select which task object's manipulation to disrupt through patch placement, without re-optimizing the patch. Our framework combines object-associated placement, differentiable physical compositing, and final action-expert representation divergence. Physical compositing accounts for perspective and occlusion across camera views, while representation divergence guides patch optimization using either relative RMS or cosine distance. Experimental results demonstrate strong attack transferability across task suites and policies, together with the ability to selectively disrupt manipulation of an attacker-chosen task object through patch placement.

title: Beyond Natural-Language Instructions: Temporal Logic as a Task Language for VLA Models with Visual-Logical Fusion
summary: Robotic tasks combine object relations, logical dependencies, and temporal requirements, which robot planning and industrial control commonly specify in temporal logic (TL). We introduce TL-VLA, a vision--language--action framework that replaces natural-language task instructions with temporal logic, making this spatiotemporal structure explicit. A typed graph encoder and visual--logical fusion condition continuous actions on the task specification and the current observations. To prepare a general vision--language backbone for this interface, we develop TL-aware robot pretraining with separate semantic and structural readouts: a frozen language teacher aligns task semantics, the structural readout encodes TL syntax to support complex, long-horizon tasks, and autoregressive action prediction connects the graph representation to robot behavior. Downstream policies inherit the pretrained backbone and TL encoder and learn new fusion and action modules. On CALVIN ABC$\rightarrow$D, our TL-aware initializer reaches \textbf{3.800} average chain length and \textbf{62.3\%} five-task success, compared with 3.578 and 54.5\% for a FAST initializer pretrained on the same data and 3.485 average chain length for a Qwen+NL baseline. On LIBERO-10, TL-aware initialization improves success from \textbf{91.2\% to 95.8\%}. On LIBERO-Mem, our policy reaches \textbf{65.0\%} success without observation history, compared with 45.0\% for a Qwen+NL reference. On held-out Panda planning specifications, it reaches \textbf{59.6\%} at Success@256 over three generation seeds, versus 48.4\% for Qwen+TL and 37.0\% for Qwen+NL. These results support explicit logical task conditioning and transferable TL-aware representations for robot action learning.

title: Inverse Reinforcement Learning with State-Dependent Foresight for Human Decision-Making
summary: Computational modeling of behavior represents individuals with a model fitted to their observed behavior and characterizes them through its parameters. Naturalistic tasks incorporate the complexity of real environments and yield high-dimensional behavioral trajectories. Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) infers the latent reward function underlying these trajectories. Standard IRL, however, assumes effectively infinite-horizon planning, whereas human foresight is both bounded and state-dependent. Here we introduce SC-AIRL (State-Conditional Adversarial IRL), which builds these two cognitive properties into the planner. Per-depth policies share one reward but differ in how far ahead they sum it explicitly. A state-conditional router mixes them according to the current state. Across held-out episodes in pedestrian crossing and highway overtaking tasks, SC-AIRL improves imitation over Standard AIRL, raising top-1 accuracy from 0.549 to 0.647 and from 0.629 to 0.718, respectively, while more closely reproducing participant behavior in rollouts. Inferred planning depth correlates with self-reported anxiety and motor impulsivity. SC-AIRL thus reproduces human behavior more closely than Standard AIRL while providing an interpretable, model-derived measure of state-dependent foresight.

title: SPARC: Semantic Calibration with Latent Multimodal Knowledge for Robust Image-Text Retrieval
summary: Robust image-text retrieval aims to maintain accurate cross-modal matching when image or text queries are incomplete, supporting reliable information access in real-world applications. However, existing methods typically focus on adapting to distribution shifts, without adequately addressing candidate discrimination for incomplete queries and ranking instability. To this end, we propose semantic projection and alignment with relational constraints (SPARC), which elicits latent multimodal knowledge from frozen encoders to improve candidate discrimination and ranking stability. Specifically, we first devise a semantic calibration module on a product of spheres that refines incomplete visual and textual features through tangent-space updates, maintaining the unit-sphere structure used for cosine similarity.
